The metrics named — monthly and annual recurring revenue, renewal rates, accounts up for renewal, overall account financial health — are subscription lifecycle measures, so the subscription and revenue lifecycle analytics dashboards are the ones that carry them. Revenue Cloud tracks the underlying values on the asset lifecycle records themselves: an asset state period holds the quantity, amount, and monthly recurring revenue for its span, and asset actions record the change in quantity, amount, and MRR, which is what these dashboards aggregate.
Order analytics reports on order volume and fulfillment rather than recurring revenue, and pricing analytics addresses how prices are being calculated and discounted rather than the state of the subscription base.
findings.note: Answer B stands as the only option covering recurring-revenue and renewal metrics, but flagged: I did not confirm the exact dashboard name 'Subscription and Revenue Lifecycle Analytics' in the documentation. The MRR-bearing objects it would aggregate are documented.

findings.explanation:
Two different limits are in play, and Revenue Cloud expresses them with two different constructs. Local cardinality sets the default, minimum, and maximum quantity allowed for an individual component, so each of T-shirts and caps gets a minimum of one and a maximum of three. Group cardinality then constrains the group the two components sit in, which is how the overall ceiling of five is imposed — without it, three plus three would allow six.
Option A sets both minimum and maximum to three on each component, which forces exactly three of each rather than allowing up to three, and then sets a group maximum of six, which is the number the requirement explicitly rules out. Option C omits caps and the group entirely, so neither the cap limit nor the combined limit exists.
One caveat: the documentation describes group cardinality as the minimum and maximum number of child components users can add, which is a count of components rather than a sum of their quantities. Option B is the intended and best-supported answer, but read the group limit as the documented component count.
findings.note: Answer B stands and is clearly the intended answer, but flagged with a precision caveat: Salesforce documents group cardinality as constraining the number of child components, not the total of their quantities, so 'total number of products should not exceed five' maps onto it only loosely.

findings.explanation:
Monthly recurring revenue is a rate, so it reflects what the customer is contracted to pay right now — not the whole deal spread thin. On January 15, 2026 the subscription is inside its first ramp year, which runs from June 24, 2025, and that year carries a quantity of 20 at US$1,000 per year. The current annual value is therefore 20 x $1,000, and dividing by the twelve months of that year gives the current MRR.
The distractors both dilute across the wrong span. Dividing the first year's value by 36 spreads one year's revenue over the entire three-year term, understating the current rate. Summing all three ramp years and dividing by 36 produces the average MRR across the whole deal, which is a different and lower figure than the rate in force today — and by construction it would never equal the MRR of any individual ramp year.
This is also why an asset state period is defined as a span holding a constant quantity, amount, and MRR: each ramp year is its own period with its own MRR, and the current one is what MRR means.
findings.note: Answer A stands. Explanation expanded from a single line to work the arithmetic and to tie the answer to the documented definition of an asset state period as a span of constant quantity, amount, and MRR, which is what makes the current ramp segment the right basis.

findings.explanation:
The lifecycle actions in the Managed Asset viewer are gated by their own API permission sets, so removing cancel from most users means unassigning the InitiateCancellation API permission and leaving it with the super users. Salesforce documents the parallel case explicitly: renewing assets from the Managed Asset viewer requires the InitiateRenewal API permission set together with Sales Rep persona permissions, and the permission table lists InitiateAmendment API, InitiateCancellation API, and InitiateRenewal API as separate permission sets granting read-write access to Asset Lifecycle objects and APIs. Because they are separate, cancel can be withdrawn without disturbing amend or renew.
Deactivating the shared amend, renew, and cancel flow would remove all three actions for everyone, not just cancel for some. A page layout change hides a control rather than revoking the ability, so a determined user or an API call would still reach the action.
findings.note: Answer B stands. Explanation expanded to cite the documented parallel — renewal requires the InitiateRenewal API permission set — and to state why the three Initiate* permission sets being separate is what makes selective removal possible.

findings.explanation:
When the same product has been bought repeatedly at different prices and part of it is later cancelled, the system has to decide which purchase the cancelled units came from. Revenue Cloud values the cancellation against the most recent asset's price, which is last in, first out.
The alternatives describe valuation methods that are coherent in accounting but are not what happens here: first in, first out would reach back to the earliest purchase price, and an averaged cost would blend every purchase into a single rate that matches none of them.
Worth flagging: I was unable to find a Salesforce article that states the drawdown order used for cancellation credits in these terms. The closest documented analogue is in Usage Management, where a product usage grant carries an explicit drawdown order with values of Expiring First, Granted First, and Granted Last — evidence that Revenue Cloud does model consumption order explicitly, but that is entitlement drawdown rather than cancellation credit.
findings.note: Answer C left in place, but COULD NOT SETTLE: no Salesforce documentation I could render states that cancellation credit is valued LIFO. The cited drawdown-order concept is from Usage Management and is adjacent rather than authoritative for this scenario.

findings.explanation:
There is one sale here, so there is one asset action — the initial assetization. The ramp is what multiplies the state periods: with Segment Type set to Yearly across a 36-month term, the subscription passes through three successive yearly segments, and because an asset state period is the span over which quantity, amount, and monthly recurring revenue stay constant, each segment is its own period. That gives one asset action and three asset state periods.
This is worth holding onto because it qualifies the usual rule. Normally an asset has as many state periods as it has changes, since each amendment adds one of each. A ramp breaks that one-to-one relationship: the periods are created up front from the ramp schedule rather than by separate transactions, so periods can outnumber actions without anything having been amended.
findings.note: Answer A stands. Explanation expanded to make explicit that a ramp decouples the usual one-state-period-per-asset-action relationship, since that is the point of the question and is also the exception to the rule cited in the non-ramped counterpart question f63e3f43.

findings.explanation:
Attribute categories render in the order the administrator defines on the attribute category records themselves, and anything not assigned to a category is collected into an Uncategorized group shown last. That gives the designer deterministic control over what a rep sees first when the configurator opens on the bundle, which matters when a product has many attributes.
The alternatives would both take that control away. Alphabetical ordering would let a rename reshuffle the configuration screen, and random ordering that varied between launches would make the configurator unusable to anyone learning a product.
findings.note: Answer B stands as the only option giving deterministic, administrator-controlled ordering, but flagged: I could not render an article that states the sequence-then-Uncategorized ordering rule explicitly.

findings.explanation:
Suspending billing on the account is the supported way to stop invoicing a delinquent customer, and it is reversible — billing resumes when the account is brought current, without anything having been destroyed. It also stops future invoices for that account only, leaving every other account's billing untouched.
Both alternatives are destructive and wrongly scoped. Deleting the invoice scheduler's scheduled jobs stops invoicing for every account the scheduler covers, not just this one, and removes the schedule the org depends on. Deleting the customer's pending invoices discards billing records rather than preventing new ones, and the next invoice run would simply generate them again.
findings.note: Answer C stands as the only non-destructive, correctly scoped option, but flagged: I could not confirm a Suspend Billing button in the documentation. The reasoning against A and B is independent of that and holds regardless.

findings.explanation:
Two requirements have to be expressed as ramp segments, and the segment types follow from the shape of each. The free first month is a Free Trial segment. The annual price increases across a minimum 36-month contract are three yearly steps, so the second segment type is Yearly — associating both to the product gives a free month followed by successive yearly segments at rising prices, which is what makes the increases visible to the customer during the sales cycle.
Monthly segments would express the same 36 months as thirty-six segments, one per month, when the price only changes once a year — far more records to maintain for an identical outcome. Custom segments exist for schedules that do not fit a regular cadence; annual increases over a three-year term are exactly regular, so Custom adds configuration effort without adding capability.
findings.note: Answer B stands. Explanation expanded from one line to say why Monthly and Custom lose — both can express the requirement, but at materially higher configuration cost, which is what makes Yearly the right answer rather than the only possible one.
